references_experience.text: frequency. 1,2,3 While the acceleration sensitivity of photonic microwave oscillators remains to be determined, the use of optical resonators rather than acoustic resonators as the basis of the oscillator operation suggests that novel methods of acoustic design and packaging that are not available to OCXOs may be pursued to overcome historical limitations. The optical frequency combs (OFCs) that underpin photonic microwave oscillators are key components in multiple other record-setting optical technologies. Optical clocks developed for position, navigation, and timing (PNT) applications employ OFCs to stabilize RF frequencies to atomic references with extreme precision over timescales of hours and beyond. While the realization of compact and rugged optical clocks for tactical military platforms remains an outstanding goal, it may be possible to significantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances

Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth electronic warfare (EW) and communications. Conventional approaches to mitigate vibration effects employ bootstrapping of multiple oscillators, active feedback, and mechanical damping or isolation, but applying these solutions requires significant added size, weight, and/or power that are not compatible with the constraints of compact, highly mobile platforms. As a result, the RF system architectures that deploy to the edge are unable to employ

ignificantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances across a platform or between physically remote RF nodes via fiber or free-space laser links. Additional implementation of OFCs for multi-wavelength communication channels offers a path to send vast data volumes over distance. DARPA’s Photonics in the Package for Extreme Scalability (PIPES) program, launched in 2019, showed that integrated photonic OFC transceivers could be co-packaged with the advanced microelectronics needed for broadband RF systems 4,5,6. Collectively, chip-scale OFCs offer multiple breakthrough functionalities to generate and distribute pure frequencies, stable time, and high- bandwidth data across and between RF systems, with the potential for novel architectures that exploit such performance to overcome performance bottlenecks inherited from electronic timing and communication standards. 1 Nakamura, T., Groman, W., Ji, Q

obile defense platforms. The program will also study the utility of additional optical device functionality such as time transfer and high-bandwidth data movement based on proposer-identified use cases. The program will rapidly develop the required componentry and system architectures necessary to take advantage of the optical timing backbone, culminating in an on-platform demonstration. At the component level, the program aims to demonstrate photonic microwave oscillators with: Phase noise < -120 dBc/Hz at 100 Hz offset 7, Phase noise < -150 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset, Relative timing error < 1 picosecond for 1–100 second intervals, and Volume < 300 cc. While RAAPTR is specifically seeking photonic approaches to microwave generation, DARPA is open to any concept that achieves program metrics. Integrated photonics, micro-optics, and/or other chip-scale photonic device approaches are not required; however, proposals for fiber-optic solutions will be closely scrutinized during proposal review for concepts that enable overcoming their susceptibility to ambient acoustic noise. Specifically excluded is research that advances non-optical methods of microwave generation or that results in evolutionary improvements to the existing state of practice. A Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) addendum provides additional details on the RAAPTR program. Please see Attachment A of this Program Solicitation (PS) for instructions on how to request the CUI Addendum. The Proposer must request the CUI Addendum by the deadline stated in the Overview section. A. Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth

AOI 01: EF Technology Sprints - Activated Digital Thread for Battlefield Responsiveness AFRL is seeking innovative solutions to operationalize digital architecture capable of responding to battlefield dynamics in near real-time. The objective is to close the loop between battlefield data and the manufacturing floor, creating an adaptive manufacturing ecosystem that expedites the re-configuration of weapon systems to enhance warfighter lethality. Solutions are sought to drastically reduce design-to-field cycle times by addressing one or more of the following technical challenges: (1) Model-Based Quality Assurance & Digital Certification. Goal: Transition from physical-test-dependent to analysis-led certification. To realize surge manufacturing, the bottleneck of physical requalification for every design change must be eliminated. Solutions are sought that leverage Certification by Analysis (CbA) and probabilistic simulation to validate manufacturing variability and design changes. Approaches should address how seamless data interchange can support certification allowing for rapid acceptance of re-configured components without extensive physical testing campaigns. (2) Modular Integration & Factorial Manufacturing. Goal: Enable "Plug-and-Play"

Driver Shifts and 24-Hour Coverage Question: The PWS mandates 24-hour operational support capability and notes that contracted vehicles with drivers shall be available to cover 12 to 24-hour services. To ensure compliance with local labor laws and accurate pricing, could you please clarify if the 24-hour support requires two physical shifts (two drivers per vehicle per day), or if drivers are expected to be on an "on-call" standby basis after an initial 12-hour shift? • Answer: The standard operating daily window is typically 12 to 18 hours, aligned with the training calendar. However, the contractor must maintain 24-hour on-call emergency response capability. To ensure compliance with local

ative runs. The contractor is responsible for all fuel, tolls, and ferry fees (speciﬁcally the balsa/ferry crossing of the Huallaga River en route to Sauce). The government will not establish a hard mileage cap, but movements will remain restricted to authorized military training and support corridors. 3. Vehicle Quantity Discrepancies Question: We noted a variance in the requested vehicle counts between the attachments and the Performance Requirements Summary (PRS)... Please conﬁrm the exact quantities required for CLINs 0003 and 0004 so we can ﬁnalize our pricing structure accordingly. • Answer: The exact quantities listed in the Schedule of Supplies/Services (CLINs) shall take precedence. The Proposer must request the CUI Addendum by the deadline stated in the Overview section. A. Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth electronic warfare (EW) and communications. Conventional approaches to mitigate vibration effects employ bootstrapping of multiple oscillators, active feedback, and mechanical damping or isolation, but applying these solutions requires significant added size, weight, and/or power that are not compatible with the constraints of compact, highly mobile platforms. As a result, the RF system architectures that deploy to the edge are unable to employ

ignificantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances across a platform or between physically remote RF nodes via fiber or free-space laser links. Additional implementation of OFCs for multi-wavelength communication channels offers a path to send vast data volumes over distance. DARPA’s Photonics in the Package for Extreme Scalability (PIPES) program, launched in 2019, showed that integrated photonic OFC transceivers could be co-packaged with the advanced microelectronics needed for broadband RF systems 4,5,6. Collectively, chip-scale OFCs offer multiple breakthrough functionalities to generate and distribute pure frequencies, stable time, and high- bandwidth data across and between RF systems, with the potential for novel architectures that exploit such performance to overcome performance bottlenecks inherited from electronic timing and communication standards. 1 Nakamura, T., Groman, W., Ji, Q

obile defense platforms. The program will also study the utility of additional optical device functionality such as time transfer and high-bandwidth data movement based on proposer-identified use cases. The program will rapidly develop the required componentry and system architectures necessary to take advantage of the optical timing backbone, culminating in an on-platform demonstration. At the component level, the program aims to demonstrate photonic microwave oscillators with: Phase noise < -120 dBc/Hz at 100 Hz offset 7, Phase noise < -150 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset, Relative timing error < 1 picosecond for 1–100 second intervals, and Volume < 300 cc. While RAAPTR is specifically seeking photonic approaches to microwave generation, DARPA is open to any concept that achieves program metrics. Integrated photonics, micro-optics, and/or other chip-scale photonic device approaches are not required; however, proposals for fiber-optic solutions will be closely scrutinized during proposal review for concepts that enable overcoming their susceptibility to ambient acoustic noise. At the system architecture level, RAAPTR aims to demonstrate not only the optical components necessary for such a backbone, but also the ancillary analog-RF and digital-RF capacity sufficient to maintain the

conducted on a Government-furnished airborne platform to verify system operation commensurate with the RAAPTR program metrics. While further system integration and functional testing (e.g., as a photonically enabled radar) is not expected to be solicited initially, DARPA intends to use the transition from Phase 1 to Phase 2 to finalize the application space of the technology, with the potential for added work based on the architectural designs developed in Phase 1. Key objectives at the system architecture level include: Maintaining oscillator performance within 3 dB across a full analog-RF transceiver chain composed of ancillary components necessary to enable a proposer-defined use case8, Developing the digital signal processing architectures and algorithm methods necessary to translate oscillator performance to relevant scenarios for mission partner transition, and Maintain performance under temperature variation -40 to 85 °C and 7.7 grms vibration, providing a path to endow the most constraining of tactical platforms with advanced RF capabilities9. C. Program Structure The RAAPTR program is a two-phase, 42-month effort. Phase 1 (24 months) will focus on component development and RF system architecture design. Phase 2 (18 months) will integrate components into a brassboard prototype for platform testing under relevant environmental conditions. Specifically excluded is research that advances non-optical methods of microwave generation or that results in evolutionary improvements to the existing state of practice. A Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) addendum provides additional details on the RAAPTR program. Please see Attachment A of this Program Solicitation (PS) for instructions on how to request the CUI Addendum. The Proposer must request the CUI Addendum by the deadline stated in the Overview section. A. Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth

AOI 01: EF Technology Sprints - Activated Digital Thread for Battlefield Responsiveness AFRL is seeking innovative solutions to operationalize digital architecture capable of responding to battlefield dynamics in near real-time. The objective is to close the loop between battlefield data and the manufacturing floor, creating an adaptive manufacturing ecosystem that expedites the re-configuration of weapon systems to enhance warfighter lethality. Solutions are sought to drastically reduce design-to-field cycle times by addressing one or more of the following technical challenges: (1) Model-Based Quality Assurance & Digital Certification. Goal: Transition from physical-test-dependent to analysis-led certification. To realize surge manufacturing, the bottleneck of physical requalification for every design change must be eliminated. Solutions are sought that leverage Certification by Analysis (CbA) and probabilistic simulation to validate manufacturing variability and design changes. Approaches should address how seamless data interchange can support certification allowing for rapid acceptance of re-configured components without extensive physical testing campaigns. (2) Modular Integration & Factorial Manufacturing. Goal: Enable "Plug-and-Play"
